scenario.name: Mandiant, ANSSI & SANS DFIR — Application Compatibility Shimcache (AppCompatCache) & Amcache.hve Triage
scenario.overview: Imagine an intruder who runs a disposable burglary tool on a server and immediately incinerates the tool afterward so no file remains on the shelf. Unbeknownst to the intruder, the operating system built-in compatibility inspector silently logs every passing binary in two separate ledgers: one ledger preserves the exact fingerprint hash and structural measurements of the vanished tool, while the second ledger records the exact chronological parade order in which tools appeared across reboots. In this scenario (T1059.003, Mandiant, ANSSI & SANS DFIR, Application Compatibility Shimcache (AppCompatCache) & Amcache.hve Triage), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: ephemeral Binary Execution, then amcache.hve InventoryApplicationFile SHA-1, then sYSTEM Hive AppCompatCache Temporal Order. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Ephemeral Binary Execution, then Amcache.hve InventoryApplicationFile SHA-1, then SYSTEM Hive AppCompatCache Temporal Order, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Ephemeral Binary Execution & Kernel ApphelpCacheControl In-Memory Tracking
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1059.003 - Windows Command Shell & AppCompat Tracking)
stages.description: The instant the intruder executes their temporary reconnaissance or dumping utility and quickly deletes it from disk, the operating system compatibility engine still quietly notes its arrival inside kernel memory to check whether legacy patches are needed. The attacker drops and executes C:\Users\Public\psexec64.exe before immediately deleting the file via del /f /q. During CreateProcessW, kernel32.dll / ntdll.dll invokes NtApphelpCacheControl to check whether the executable requires application compatibility shims, inserting an entry into the kernel in-memory LRU Shimcache table (logged in Sysmon Event 1 with ExecutablePath=C:\Users\Public\psexec64.exe, KernelSubsystem=NtApphelpCacheControl , Win10/11 10ts magic header, AntiForensicAction=del /f /q C:\Users\Public\psexec64.exe so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes C:\Users\Public\psexec64.exe -accepteula \\10.10.0.10 cmd.exe (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , C:\Users\Public\psexec64.exe -accepteula \\10.10.0.10 cmd.exe via psexec64.exe, passing the so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1059.003 during "Ephemeral Binary Execution & Kernel ApphelpCacheControl In-Memory Tracking" , The attacker drops and executes C:\Users\Public\psexec64 while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact del /f /q C:\Users\Public\psexec64.exe runs (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , del /f /q C:\Users\Public\psexec64.exe via psexec64.exe, passing the exact arguments, target so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1059.003 during "Ephemeral Binary Execution & Kernel ApphelpCacheControl In-Memory Tracking" , The attacker drops and executes C:\Users\Public\psexec64 while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). stages.title: Stage 2: Amcache.hve InventoryApplicationFile SHA-1 Hash & PE Header Persistence
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1070.004 - File Deletion Defeated by Amcache.hve SHA-1)
stages.description: Opening the dedicated Application Inventory ledger kept by the operating system, forensic analysts recover the exact cryptographic fingerprint, file size, and compilation date of the deleted attacker binary so they can match it straight against global threat intelligence. Concurrently, the Application Experience service (aelupsvc / CompatTelRunner.exe) writes a permanent record into C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve under Root\InventoryApplicationFile\psexec64.exe|<Hash>, storing the lowercased full path, FileId (0000 + SHA-1 hash of the first 31.4 MB of the binary), LinkDate (PE compile timestamp), and BinaryType (logged in WinEvent Event 100 with ForensicHive=C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve, RegistrySubKey=Root\InventoryApplicationFile, RecoveredSha1=a94a8fe5ccb19ba61c4c0873d391e987982fbbd3 , FileId strip 0000, KeyLastWriteUtc=2026-11-03 09:14:22.810 so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes AmcacheParser.exe -f "C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve" --csv C:\Forensics (which Extracts and parses persistent Windows execution artifacts from HKLM\SYSTEM AppCompatCache , ShimCache, C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve so that reconstructs historical binary execution, SHA-1 file hashes, run counts, last execution timestamps, and per-process network bytes sent , T1070.004 during "Amcache.hve InventoryApplicationFile SHA-1 Hash & PE Header Persistence" even after the attacker deletes the malware executable from disk). Next, the follow-up artifact Hive Key: Amcache.hve\Root\InventoryApplicationFile\psexec64.exe|f8192a01b2c3d4e5 runs (which Extracts and parses persistent Windows execution artifacts from HKLM\SYSTEM AppCompatCache , ShimCache, C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve so that reconstructs historical binary execution, SHA-1 file hashes, run counts, last execution timestamps, and per-process network bytes sent , T1070.004 during "Amcache.hve InventoryApplicationFile SHA-1 Hash & PE Header Persistence" even after the attacker deletes the malware executable from disk). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ AmcacheParser.exe -f C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve --nl false / ⇠#2 ACK 100) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Kernel ApphelpCacheControl), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Amcache.hve (SHA-1 FileId)).

stages.title: Stage 3: SYSTEM Hive AppCompatCache (10ts Signature) Temporal Order Reconstruction
stages.subtitle: Discovery (T1083 - Chronological Execution Reconstruction via Shimcache)
stages.description: Next, analysts examine the SYSTEM Compatibility Cache ribbon stamped with its signature 10ts header, reading the exact ordered sequence of binaries to reconstruct which tools ran right before and right after the deleted payload. Parsing HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache with AppCompatCacheParser.exe extracts the Windows 10/11 "10ts" (0x31 0x30 0x74 0x73) binary structure. The CacheEntryPosition index reveals the exact chronological order in which psexec64.exe was evaluated relative to neighboring processes (logged in WinEvent Event 101 with RegistryKey=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache, HeaderSignature=10ts , 0x31307473 Windows 10/11/Server 2019+, CacheEntryPosition=14 , MRU Order, ExecutedFlag=Yes so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes AppCompatCacheParser.exe -f "C:\Windows\System32\config\SYSTEM" --csv C:\Forensics (which Extracts and parses persistent Windows execution artifacts from HKLM\SYSTEM AppCompatCache , ShimCache, C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve so that reconstructs historical binary execution, SHA-1 file hashes, run counts, last execution timestamps, and per-process network bytes sent , T1083 during "SYSTEM Hive AppCompatCache , 10ts Signature Temporal Order Reconstruction" even after the attacker deletes the malware executable from disk). Next, the follow-up artifact Registry Value: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache\AppCompatCache runs (which Modifies or queries Windows Registry keys and values , Registry Value: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache\AppComp so that extracts the 16-byte SysKey / BootKey , stored across the JD, Skew1, GBG, and Data registry classes under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa required to decrypt the PEK and password hashes inside ntds.dit or SAM , T1083). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ AppCompatCacheParser.exe -f C:\Windows\System32\config\SYSTEM / ⇠#3 ACK 101) from Node ③ (#3 Kernel ApphelpCacheControl) to Node ④ (#4 SYSTEM Hive (AppCompatCache)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Amcache.hve (SHA-1 FileId)).

keySpecs.value: Correlate AppCompatCache CacheEntryPosition ordering with Amcache.hve KeyLastWriteTimestamp and SHA-1 hashes to prove binary presence and execution even when event logs and files are wiped.

steps.howItWorksInPractice: Under the hood, the observed step executes AppCompatCacheParser.exe -f "C:\Windows\System32\config\SYSTEM" --csv C:\Forensics (which Extracts and parses persistent Windows execution artifacts from HKLM\SYSTEM AppCompatCache , ShimCache, C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve so that reconstructs historical binary execution, SHA-1 file hashes, run counts, last execution timestamps, and per-process network bytes sent , T1083 during "SYSTEM Hive AppCompatCache , 10ts Signature Temporal Order Reconstruction" even after the attacker deletes the malware executable from disk). Next, the follow-up artifact Registry Value: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache\AppCompatCache runs (which Modifies or queries Windows Registry keys and values , Registry Value: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache\AppComp so that extracts the 16-byte SysKey / BootKey , stored across the JD, Skew1, GBG, and Data registry classes under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa required to decrypt the PEK and password hashes inside ntds.dit or SAM , T1083).
steps.diagramAlignment: On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 across the topology from Self-Deleting Tool , psexec64 and Kernel ApphelpCacheControl toward SYSTEM Hive , AppCompatCache and AppCompatCacheParser & Amcache.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Documented in WinEvent Event 101 (recording RegistryKey=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache, HeaderSignature=10ts , 0x31307473 Windows 10/11/Server 2019+, CacheEntryPosition=14 , MRU Order, ExecutedFlag=Yes under T1083): Correlate AppCompatCache CacheEntryPosition ordering with Amcache.hve KeyLastWriteTimestamp and SHA-1 hashes to prove binary presence and execution even when event logs and files are wiped.
